Christine Ebersole as Elizabeth Arden and Patti LuPone as Helena Rubinstein in "War Paint." Credit: Joan Marcus WHERE Nederlander Theatre, 208 W. 41st St. INFO $69-$179; 877-250-2929, warpaintmusical.com BOTTOM LINE A good musical and a marvelous showcase for Patti LuPone and Christine Ebersole.
On a Broadway stage, with a zinger to deliver and a song to put across, they and their formidable talents are absolutely ageless.

Each respective performance is of a wattage ample to send home the patron feeling like existential revelation was imbued in those final moments, even if the women's affect on us all remains, well, overly concealed.
The 'Grey Gardens' team is reunited and in good form here.

Two singing actresses at the peak of their powers, a fascinating premise, knockout costumes, and a score (beautifully orchestrated by Bruce Coughlin) that is destined to make a great cast album: So why is the show as a whole less than great?
Yes, it’s entertaining enough, but nothing like the deckle-edged hit it wants so desperately to be, and the reasons why it fails to come off are worth a close look.
War Paint's nails, though attractively polished, only scratch its surface.
Somehow this all manages to be a huge bore though not for want of trying and effortful lung power from the leads in director Michael Greif’s high-voltage production.

The musical about cosmetics titans Helena Rubinstein and Elizabeth Arden has two powerhouse performers in Patti LuPone and Christine Ebersole, but even they can't rescue this overstuffed and undercooked show.

"Ebersole and LuPone are nothing short of flawless...Add a heaping pile of beauty, glamour and lush costumes to the mix, and you have yourself a juicy — albeit highly elegant — drama...The music is strong but not particularly memorable...But the lyrics are impactful...

Sophisticated, chic and elegant, War Paint is an absorbing and magnificent story of two remarkable women who climbed their way to the top of their profession only to find that there were still things they could not accomplish.

What’s compelling is the character driven plot giving insight into the lives of two unusual women who created empires at a time when it was unfashionable and unacceptable – – the chosen twosome are unparalleled in talent and star power.
These ladies who wear hats but do much more than lunch are knockouts.
“War Paint,” mostly, is bliss and makeup.

First, there's the industrial rise and (inevitably) the decline of these two hyper-ambitious, ultra-determined women, in a business world even more strongly male-dominated than today's. Within that story, there's their personal rivalry, fueled partly by a catty resentment that allows Doug Wright to spangle his script with smart, caustic zingers.
War Paint still has a lot going for it, including self-empowered protagonists, high-powered performances, well-crafted period-style songs.
Unfortunately, that rather touching finale comes too late to save this musicalized, fact-based feud from being a rather hum-drum addition to the current line-up of new Broadway musicals
“An important story that's certainly worthy of a first class treatment, and director Michael Greif's polished and professional production delivers...
For all its appeal, 'War Paint' does not surmount some logistical problems that are likely to make some of the scenes heavy-going
LuPone, balancing classical gusto with characteristic bravura, and Ebersole, sweetly and openly alive in show stopping musical numbers, are legendary.
Just not much of a stunner under the makeup.
They're so good, you wish the show were better.
Anyone heading into "War Paint" looking for "Valley of the Dolls"-style hair-pulling -- or even "Dynasty"
War Paint is a show that wants to be many things—a celebration of female empowerment, a meditation on beauty and aging, a business saga—but never quite decides which of these it wants to be most.
After a shaky opening, War Paint heats up in the second act.
But "War Paint" could have done with a little less panache — and a lot more plot.
A lot of very fine work -- by some very gifted people -- has gone into 'War Paint,' but it adds up to little more than a skirmish.
They’re so good, you wish the show were better.
But there is no disguising that there was no way to make this musical into more than a star vehicle with wobbly wheels.
But none of it can compensate for a story that is fundamentally inert.
And everyone wins, especially the audience.
These two powerhouse performers deliver dazzling vocals, emotional depth, and palpable energy.
After seeing so many movies turned into mediocre musicals, I can honestly say it was a thrill to enjoy this gem of an original musical.
In addition, I found both productions tremendously satisfying.
You'll hardly feel that you've wasted your money on some totally useless product.
For the most part, War Paint is smart and marvelously stylish entertainment.

War Paint may not be a great musical but it gives us the opportunity to see two great stage performers show off their talents, with two strong supporting men in the cast and a story about the obstacles women have faced.
The actresses starring as the makeup mavens are no powder puffs themselves: Patti LuPone as Rubinstein and Christian Ebersole as Arden.
If you're eager to see two dueling divas conquer the cosmetics industry, run to the box office.
Doug Wright’s book makes the most of opportunities for bitchy one-liners but provides little tension as the twin plots unfurl across the decades.
War Paint is redeemed by its packaging, specifically the powerhouse team of Tony Award winners Patti LuPone and Christine Ebersole.
"The music by Scott Frankel and lyrics by Michael Korie work best when sung by the stars, and director Michael Greif has worked hard to keep up a pace in a show that seems over-extended...
It's also a drawn-out cat fight whose self-conscious interrogations of gender often ring tone-deaf.
It’s full of high energy and big performances—and yet it manages to feel nearly as empty as used-up tub of face cream.
Too bad that the show doesn’t sparkle nearly as much and it could have, for LuPone has the right flash of authority.
The whole is less than the sum of its parts.

It is a shame that the musical, despite beautiful costumes and pleasant music and terrific performances by Christine Ebersole as Arden and Patti LuPone as Rubinstein, rarely goes more than skin-deep in its exploration of this fascinating duo.
Sadly, however, this musical may not win over any new customers.
Even the power and polish of the two leads could not keep me from longing for this thing to end.
A quick look at their biographies suggests what War Paint might have been, instead of (dare I say it) what it mostly is -- dull as dirt.

cn.t: Critics praise powerhouse performances from LuPone and Ebersole, but find the musical itself superficial and dramatically inert. The stars dazzle in a dual showcase that's visually stunning yet only skin-deep, lacking the substance to match its glamorous packaging.

sg.ra: The Nederlander is a relatively compact 1,232-seat 1921 Walter C. Jordan house (architect William Neil Smith) with a shallow orchestra rake, so you want to sit forward of where the problems begin; center rows B-E sit forward of the mezz overhang (which becomes notable at row M) and forward of where the shallow rake starts costing shorter patrons their sightlines, giving a direct center look at the 86-ft-wide stage.

sg.vl: Smart value under the overhang line
sg.ra: The Nederlander mezz overhang is 'notable by row M and cuts into the stage at row Q,' so center rows L-O sit just on the safe side of that line - you get a sub-premium price in a 1921 house known historically for being overlooked on its lone 41st Street block (the southernmost Broadway theater), without the shallow-rake head-blocking that plagues the back half.

sg.vl: Where the overhang eats the stage
sg.ra: This is the Nederlander-specific trap: the mezz overhang 'cuts into the stage at row Q,' and the 1921 orchestra's shallow rake means a tall patron in front of you is a real problem - one Redwood patron reported the overhang 'cuts off about the top 20% of the stage,' which mattered because that show featured climbing a redwood; skip for anything with vertical staging or flying effects.

The Nederlander's mezz is raked steeply enough that sightlines stay clean even though you're in a 1921 house without an elevator - rows BB and CC beat row AA because AA has a safety bar across the front that 'may be too high for shorter theatergoers' and 'can cut into the stage'; the center front mezz here looks down into the 40-ft proscenium cleanly.

Multiple guides single out the last two front-mezz rows (DD, EE) as the best 'value for money' at the Nederlander - you're still in the front mezz bloc with the steep mezz rake that keeps the 1921 house's sightlines clean, but priced below rows AA-CC; the tradeoff is legroom which is tight across the mezz here.

The Nederlander has no balcony - the rear mezz is the top tier - and the house is a compact 1,232 seats, so even the 'farthest' seat isn't far; the mezz rake stays steep enough that middle seats FF-JJ hold up, and this is the southernmost Broadway theater (208 W 41st, unusually isolated from the 44th-45th Street cluster), which typically keeps these prices lower than comparable rear-mezz at flagship houses.

sg.vl: Last rows of a no-elevator house
sg.ra: The Nederlander has 'no elevators or escalators' - a 1921 house quirk that matters when you're climbing to rows KK-PP - and a Tripadvisor thread flagged that row JJ sits above a stairwell entryway with a railing bar that can intrude; beyond JJ you're in the last stretch of a 10-row rear mezz (FF-PP) with tight legroom and the most angled sightlines in the house, and this is the top tier since there's no balcony.
